projectTitle: Veridian Holdings: One Trusted Definition, Found the Hard Way
projectTagline: A 20-video, start-to-finish Microsoft Purview governance build for a fictional multi-division conglomerate -- registering five disconnected systems, resolving a three-way customer-count conflict into two honestly separate terms instead of one forced blend, assigning named ownership, and surfacing a real classification gap through audit, not a demo script.
businessContext: Veridian Holdings runs three divisions -- Retail, Logistics, and Financial Services -- on five disconnected systems: an Azure SQL Database for core transactions, Salesforce for CRM, Oracle Financials for accounting, a Snowflake warehouse, and a Fabric lakehouse feeding the executive Power BI dashboard. Finance, Marketing, and the warehouse team have each reported a different "Active Customer" count for years, nobody owns most of the data, sensitive columns have never been systematically classified, and no one can trace a dashboard number back to its source. This series builds a real Microsoft Purview governance program to fix all four, using Veridian's actual systems and actual people throughout.
architectureSummary: Microsoft Purview as the governance domain of record: Data Map registration and scanning across all five sources, a Business Glossary with Active Customer and Engaged Account as separately governed terms, RACI-style ownership by domain (Customer, Financial, Product/Inventory) entered directly on Purview Contacts, Confidential-PII sensitivity labeling, automated lineage from source systems through a Fabric dataflow and lakehouse to the executive Power BI dashboard, Purview Data Quality rules enforcing the two approved definitions and Net Revenue, and a governance-reporting pipeline feeding both an access-policy audit trail and a nightly Council scorecard.

lessons.title: Meeting Veridian Holdings: Why Nobody Can Say Who Owns Customer Data
lessons.summary: The discovery meeting: an internal audit question nobody could answer exposes that five systems, three conflicting customer counts, and zero documented data owners are really one underlying governance failure.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Over the next 20 videos, you'll build a real Microsoft Purview governance program for a fictional multi-division conglomerate, Veridian Holdings -- three divisions (Retail, Logistics, and Financial Services) running on five disconnected systems: an Azure SQL Database (veridian-sql-prod) for core transactions, Salesforce for CRM, an Oracle Financials instance for accounting, a Snowflake warehouse, and a Microsoft Fabric lakehouse feeding Power BI dashboards. Across those five systems sit roughly 2.1 million customer identities, no two systems counting them quite the same way, and nobody who can tell you, with confidence, who is formally accountable for any one of them.

This video starts where a governance engagement actually starts: not with a Purview license, a scan, or a glossary term, but with the meeting where the real shape of the problem gets named out loud. You'll meet the Chief Data Officer who sponsored this work, the division leaders whose numbers don't agree, and the audit finding that turned "we should probably look into this someday" into a funded program with a deadline.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a huge house with five different storage rooms, and over the years, different people filled each room without ever talking to each other. Nobody wrote down, on any door, whose stuff is actually in each room, or who's supposed to take care of it. So when someone asks how many winter coats the house owns, one room says 40, another room says 55, and a third room says 48 -- and all three people counting are telling the truth about their own room, they just counted differently.

Now imagine someone official, like an inspector, comes by and asks a scarier question: show me every room where you keep the family's social security cards, and tell me exactly who has a key to each one. Nobody in the house can answer that completely, not because anyone did anything wrong, but because nobody ever wrote any of it down. That's the exact moment that gets Veridian Holdings to finally pay someone to walk through every room, write down what's in it, and put a name on the door.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the discovery phase of a data governance engagement, and like most governance engagements, the thing that actually got budget approved wasn't an abstract desire for better data quality -- it was a specific, uncomfortable audit finding. Veridian's VP of Compliance asked a routine-sounding question during an internal controls review: show me everywhere a customer's Social Security number is stored today, and exactly who can access each location. Nobody in the room -- not Finance, not the CRM team, not the data platform group -- could answer that completely, and the gap between "we're pretty sure" and "here's the verified list" is what finally got this program funded.

Underneath that single audit question are four distinct, compounding gaps that you need to name precisely in this first meeting, because each one gets a different fix later in this series: no documented ownership (nobody is formally accountable for any of the five systems or the critical data elements inside them), no agreed definitions (Oracle Financials, Salesforce, and the Snowflake warehouse each report a different active-customer count, and all three are internally defensible), no classification (nobody has systematically identified which columns, across which systems, actually hold SSNs or other sensitive financial details), and no lineage (nobody can trace a number on the executive Power BI dashboard back through Fabric, through Snowflake, to whichever source system actually produced it).

Your job in this meeting is the same discipline as any other discovery session: don't propose a fix yet. Extract each stakeholder's number, their reasoning, and their honest answer to who owns this system, in their own words, because the specific shape of the disagreement is what every later lesson in this series, from the critical-data-element inventory to the Purview classification scan, is built to resolve.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Walk in already knowing the four gaps you're listening for

Before the meeting, write down the four distinct failures hiding behind "we don't trust our data":

- Is there a named, accountable owner for each system and its critical data elements, or does everyone just assume IT owns all of it by default?
- Do Active Customer, Net Revenue, and similar terms mean the same thing in every system that reports them?
- Has anyone systematically identified which columns, in which systems, actually contain SSNs or other sensitive financial data?
- Can anyone trace a number on the executive dashboard back to the specific source system and table it came from?

## Step 2 -- Let the audit finding open the meeting

Monica Alvarez, Veridian's Chief Data Officer, called this meeting, and she hands it straight to the person who actually triggered it:

```
GRACE OKONKWO (VP of Compliance & Internal Audit): During the last
  controls review I asked a simple question: show me everywhere a
  customer's SSN is stored today, and exactly who can access each
  location. Nobody could give me a complete answer. Not an estimate --
  a verified list. That's what's funding this.
MONICA: And that's not a one-time embarrassment. If we can't answer
  that question today, we can't answer it the next time someone
  asks, either -- a regulator, an acquirer, a customer.
```

## Step 3 -- Interview each system owner separately, starting with their number

```
DANIEL REYES (Finance Director, owns Oracle Financials / ORACLE_FIN):
  "438,000 active customers. Anyone with a paid transaction in the
  trailing 12 months. That's what goes to the board."

LENA FITZGERALD (VP of Marketing & CRM Operations, owns Salesforce):
  "561,000. Active means engaged -- an open opportunity or marketing
  touch in the last 90 days. Billing status doesn't tell me who to
  target."

VICTOR KESSLER (Director of Data Platform Engineering, owns
  veridian-sql-prod, VERIDIAN_DW, and the Fabric lakehouse):
  "Snowflake's blended number is 497,000. Honestly, I inherited that
  join logic. I couldn't tell you today exactly how it reconciles
  Oracle and Salesforce, or whether it should."
```

## Step 4 -- Ask the ownership question directly, and listen for the silence

```
YOU: Daniel, if I have a question about a specific customer record in
     Oracle Financials six months from now, who do I go to?
DANIEL: Technically... me? But nobody's ever asked me to formally
        sign off on that.
YOU: Victor, same question for the Snowflake warehouse number.
VICTOR: That's the problem. I maintain the pipeline. I'm not sure
        that makes me the owner of what the number means.
```

That hesitation -- not a wrong answer, just an honest admission that nobody's actually confirmed it -- is the real finding of this meeting.

## Step 5 -- Write the one-page discovery findings artifact

```
VERIDIAN HOLDINGS -- GOVERNANCE DISCOVERY FINDINGS

Systems in scope: veridian-sql-prod (Azure SQL), Salesforce (CRM),
ORACLE_FIN (Oracle Financials), VERIDIAN_DW (Snowflake), Fabric
lakehouse -> Power BI executive dashboard.

GAP 1 -- Ownership: no system or critical data element has a
  formally confirmed, documented owner.
GAP 2 -- Definition: Active Customer produces three different,
  individually defensible numbers (438K / 561K / 497K).
GAP 3 -- Classification: sensitive columns (SSNs, financial detail)
  have never been systematically identified across any of the five
  systems.
GAP 4 -- Lineage: no documented trail from the executive dashboard
  back to its originating source system.
```

## Step 6 -- Flag the audit exposure separately from the definition conflict

The SSN question is not the same kind of problem as the three conflicting customer counts, and it shouldn't get buried inside that debate:

```
COMPLIANCE EXPOSURE (not a definitional disagreement):
  Grace's audit question could not be fully answered. Victor's team
  can identify likely SSN columns in Oracle Financials and
  veridian-sql-prod, but has not verified Salesforce, and has never
  produced a complete, access-mapped inventory. Carried forward as
  the top-priority input to the classification work scoped in
  Lesson 3.
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Ran discovery across all five Veridian systems. Confirmed three internally reasonable but conflicting Active Customer counts (438K Oracle, 561K Salesforce, 497K Snowflake), zero formally documented data owners anywhere, and an unverified SSN footprint that failed a direct compliance question. None of this is one team's fault -- it's the absence of any governance layer across systems that were each built independently.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We met with the CDO, Compliance, Finance, Marketing, and Data Platform leads and documented, specifically, why Veridian can't answer basic questions about its own customer data. This session also surfaced the actual trigger for the program's funding -- an audit question nobody could answer -- which gives us a concrete, board-visible reason to point back to for every decision ahead.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We now know exactly why a routine audit question about customer SSNs couldn't be answered last quarter: nobody owns the data, three systems define customer three different ways, and there's no record of where sensitive information actually lives. That's documented in writing now, which is the first real step toward being able to answer that question with confidence next time.

lessons.title: Turning "Fix Our Trust Problem" Into a Testable Governance Requirement
lessons.summary: Converting four discovery findings -- no ownership, no agreed definitions, no classification, no lineage -- into four written, verifiable governance requirements that Finance, Marketing, and Compliance all sign off on.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 1 named four real gaps at Veridian Holdings: no documented ownership, three conflicting Active Customer numbers, no systematic classification of sensitive data, and no lineage trail from the executive dashboard back to its source. That's an accurate diagnosis, but "we should fix our trust problem" is not something you can build a governance program against -- it's not specific enough to know when it's actually done. This video turns each of those four gaps into one precise, written requirement, specific enough that someone could check it against real Veridian data and get an unambiguous yes or no.

These four requirements are the document every later lesson in this series answers to. When you build the critical-data-element inventory, register sources in Purview's Data Map, apply sensitivity labels, or trace a dashboard number back to its source, you're implementing against exactly these four sentences -- not a vague mandate that gets re-argued every time someone asks whether this is actually governed yet.
lessons.explainSimple:
Remember the house with five storage rooms and three different coat counts? Now imagine the family sits down together and writes an actual rulebook: every room gets a name card on the door saying who's responsible for it, everyone counts coats only one way and writes it down, and if one room's count means something different, it gets a different name instead of an argument about whose number is real. Any room with important papers in it gets a special red sticker, with a list of exactly who has a key.

The hard part isn't agreeing the rulebook sounds fair -- it's writing each rule specific enough that anyone could walk through the house later and check, room by room, whether the rule is actually being followed. A rule like "be more careful with important papers" doesn't work. A rule like "every room holding papers with a social security number gets a red sticker, and the sticker lists every single person with a key" does.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A governance requirement that sounds reasonable in a steering committee meeting and a governance requirement that's actually verifiable are two different artifacts, and most "we agreed on governance" initiatives quietly fail in that gap. The test is the same discipline as a data-quality test: for every clause, there has to be a concrete way to check it against real Veridian data and get a definite answer. "We'll take ownership more seriously" is not verifiable. "Every critical data element has exactly one named Data Owner and at least one named Data Steward, recorded in the stewardship matrix, confirmed in writing by that person" is verifiable -- someone can open the matrix, pick any element, and check.

The same discipline applies to the definition conflict. Rather than declaring one of Daniel's, Lena's, or Victor's numbers simply wrong, the better resolution -- discovered by working through the requirement with them directly -- is to recognize that Finance and Marketing were never actually measuring the same thing. Daniel's billing-basis number becomes the one canonical, Purview-published Active Customer glossary term. Lena's engagement-basis number gets its own name, Engaged Account, preserved as a real and useful metric instead of forced into a fight it was never going to win cleanly. Victor's Snowflake blended number, once its undocumented join logic is examined, turns out to answer a question nobody actually needs answered once the other two are properly named and governed.

The classification and lineage requirements need the same rigor. "Classify sensitive data" isn't verifiable; "every column in any of the five systems identified as containing an SSN or financial account detail carries the Confidential – PII sensitivity label, confirmed by a completed scan coverage report" is. "Document lineage" isn't verifiable; "any figure labeled Active Customer on the executive Power BI dashboard can be traced, hop by hop, back through the Fabric semantic model and Snowflake to ORACLE_FIN, the one approved source" is -- because someone can actually pick a number and walk it back by hand.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Pull every testable claim out of the Lesson 1 findings

```
FROM DISCOVERY:
  - No system or critical data element has a confirmed owner
  - Active Customer means three different, individually valid
    things depending on the system
  - Sensitive columns (SSN, financial detail) have never been
    systematically identified anywhere
  - No one can trace a dashboard number back to its source system
```

## Step 2 -- Draft the four candidate requirements

```
REQ-1 (Ownership): Every critical data element at Veridian has
  exactly one named Data Owner and at least one named Data Steward,
  recorded in the stewardship matrix, with written confirmation from
  that person.

REQ-2 (Glossary): Active Customer has one approved definition,
  published in the Purview business glossary, sourced from one
  authoritative system. Any other existing count is either retired
  or renamed to reflect what it actually measures.

REQ-3 (Classification): Every column across all five systems
  containing an SSN or financial account detail carries the
  Confidential – PII sensitivity label, confirmed by a completed
  Purview scan coverage report, not a sampled or partial one.

REQ-4 (Lineage): Any figure labeled Active Customer on the executive
  Power BI dashboard can be traced hop by hop -- dashboard, semantic
  model, Fabric lakehouse, Snowflake, source system -- back to its
  one approved origin.
```

## Step 3 -- Pressure-test REQ-2 live, in the room

```
DANIEL: My billing number is the one the board already trusts. I'm
        not comfortable calling anything else Active Customer.
LENA: Then don't. Call mine something else -- Engaged Account. I
      don't actually need the word Customer in my metric name, I
      need my own number to keep existing and be respected.
YOU: Agreed. One canonical Active Customer, billing basis, published
     in the glossary. Engaged Account becomes its own named,
     equally governed metric -- not a rejected one.
VICTOR: Then what happens to Snowflake's blended number?
YOU: Once Active Customer and Engaged Account are both properly
     defined and owned, does anyone still need a third blended one?
VICTOR: ...Honestly, no. I think that number only ever existed
        because nobody had settled this.
```

## Step 4 -- Write each requirement with a named owner and a verification method, then version it

Save as `Veridian_Governance_Requirements_v1.md`, dated, with Monica Alvarez, Daniel Reyes, Lena Fitzgerald, Victor Kessler, and Grace Okonkwo each named against the requirement their system or role is accountable for.

## Step 5 -- Get an explicit yes from each person, clause by clause

Don't treat meeting silence as agreement. Read REQ-1 through REQ-4 aloud and ask each stakeholder directly whether it matches what they need -- Grace's sign-off on REQ-3 and REQ-4 matters most, since those two are what let her answer the audit question completely next time it's asked.

## Step 6 -- Walk one real example through all four requirements before the meeting ends

```
EXAMPLE: A single Veridian customer record appears in ORACLE_FIN
  (paid in the last 12 months), Salesforce (no engagement in 90
  days), and VERIDIAN_DW.
  REQ-2 result: counted in Active Customer (billing basis), NOT
    counted in Engaged Account. Daniel and Lena both confirm this
    matches intent.
  REQ-3 result: if this record's Oracle row includes an SSN column,
    that column must already carry Confidential – PII once REQ-3
    ships -- Victor flags this as the one he's least confident is
    fully covered today.
```

That last admission from Victor -- a specific, named uncertainty about SSN coverage -- is exactly the kind of gap this requirement is designed to surface before the classification work in Lesson 3 begins.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Converted four discovery gaps into four written, verifiable requirements -- ownership, glossary, classification, and lineage -- each with a named accountable person and a concrete way to check it against real data. Resolved the Active Customer conflict by splitting it into two correctly-named metrics rather than declaring a winner, and got explicit sign-off from every stakeholder, including Compliance on the two requirements that matter most to the next audit.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We now have four signed, specific governance requirements instead of a general mandate to fix our trust problem. Each one has an owner and a way to verify it's actually done, which gives us a clean definition of done for V1 instead of an argument that resurfaces every status meeting.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Finance and Marketing's conflicting customer numbers turned out to be two different, both-useful metrics that were never named correctly -- that's resolved in writing now. We also have a specific, checkable commitment for exactly how Compliance's audit question gets answered going forward.

lessons.title: Scoping V1: Catalog and Classify Now, Quality Rules and MDM Next
lessons.summary: Drawing a hard, written line around what the first phase of the governance program actually delivers -- cataloging, ownership, and classification -- while sequencing data quality rules and master data management into the same engagement, not a separate future one.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
You now have four signed, verifiable requirements covering ownership, a single Active Customer definition, classification, and lineage. That's enough to start planning the actual governance platform -- but not enough to start building it, because "fix our trust problem" quietly contains several more projects that surfaced the moment five stakeholders sat in two meetings together. This video draws a hard written line around V1: what ships in this first phase, and what gets explicitly sequenced into later phases of this same engagement rather than silently dropped or pushed into some future project that never gets funded.

This scope document is what you'll point back to a few lessons from now, when Monica Alvarez, excited that Active Customer finally has one trustworthy number, asks whether you can also just fix the duplicate customer records sitting across Oracle and Salesforce while you're already in there.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a garage so disorganized that nobody can find anything, and everyone wants it fixed at once -- label every box, throw out duplicates, build better shelves, and make sure nothing dangerous is left lying around. Trying to do all of that on the same Saturday means nothing actually gets finished. The smart move is to label every box and flag the dangerous stuff first, because you genuinely can't safely combine two boxes of duplicate items until you know for certain what's actually in each one.

So you write two lists: this is what we're doing this weekend -- labeling and flagging -- and this is next weekend, same project, already scheduled -- organizing shelves and merging duplicates. Nothing gets forgotten, but the most urgent and most dangerous part gets handled first.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is scope management applied specifically to a governance engagement, and the expansion pressure here has a particular shape: once a sponsor sees one trustworthy, governed number, their appetite for more governed things grows immediately, because trust in one outcome creates demand for the next one. That's a healthy sign the program is working, but it still needs the same discipline as any scope boundary -- every request gets an explicit disposition, never a silent drop, because an unaddressed request doesn't disappear, it resurfaces later as a surprise that erodes the same trust you're building.

At Veridian, the V1 boundary separates what the rest of the program structurally depends on from what has to be built on top of it. Registering and scanning all five systems in Purview's Data Map, assigning a confirmed owner and steward to every critical data element, publishing the Active Customer glossary definition, and applying Confidential – PII labels to every sensitive column are foundational -- get any of these wrong and everything downstream inherits the error. Writing data quality rules (SQL checks that continuously verify the Active Customer calculation stays correct) and master data management work (actually merging the duplicate customer records Victor's team already knows exist across Oracle and Salesforce) are both real, valuable, and explicitly part of this same engagement -- but they depend on the catalog and classification being solid first. You cannot safely write a quality rule for a critical data element nobody has formally identified yet, and you cannot safely merge records across systems until you know, with certainty, which fields are sensitive and who's accountable for each source.


## Step 3 -- Write the V1 scope statement

```
VERIDIAN GOVERNANCE PROGRAM -- V1 SCOPE

Ships in V1:
  - All five sources registered and scanned in Purview's Data Map
  - Critical data element inventory (customer PII + the elements
    behind Active Customer)
  - Ownership + stewardship RACI, signed by name, for every CDE
  - Active Customer glossary term published and approved; Engaged
    Account published as its own separate metric
  - Confidential – PII labels applied to every confirmed sensitive
    column
  - Lineage documentation for the Active Customer figure, source
    to executive dashboard

Sequenced next, same engagement (not deferred to a separate future
project):
  - Phase 2 -- data quality rules and SQL checks
  - Phase 3 -- master data management / duplicate customer merge

Logged, not yet scheduled:
  - Retention policy
  - AI governance framework
```

## Step 4 -- Rehearse the scope-creep conversation before it happens mid-build

```
MONICA: Since your team's already in Oracle and Salesforce, can we
        just merge the duplicate customer records too?
YOU:    We can -- it's already Phase 3 on this same engagement, not
        a separate ask. But merging records today means guessing at
        which fields are sensitive and whose data we're even
        combining, because the classification and ownership work
        isn't finished yet. I'd rather hand Phase 3 a trustworthy
        catalog to merge against than rush both and have you doubt
        the merged records the same way you doubt today's numbers.
```

## Step 5 -- Get written sign-off on the full sequence, not just V1

Attach the V1 scope statement to the Lesson 2 requirements document and get one explicit confirmation from Monica covering both the V1 boundary and the Phase 2/Phase 3 sequence -- this is the document you reopen when quality rules and MDM formally begin later in this engagement.

## Step 6 -- Name the order sources get registered in within V1

```
REGISTRATION ORDER:
  1. ORACLE_FIN first -- highest compliance exposure, since it's
     the system most directly tied to Grace's audit question.
  2. veridian-sql-prod second -- core transactional PII, closely
     related exposure.
  3. Salesforce third -- CRM data, lower sensitivity but needed to
     resolve the Active Customer vs. Engaged Account split.
  4. VERIDIAN_DW fourth -- depends on the first three being scanned
     to classify correctly, since it blends their data.
  5. Fabric lakehouse / Power BI last -- lineage only means anything
     once every upstream source is already cataloged.
```

Data quality rules and MDM are both explicitly sequenced into this same engagement as Phase 2 and Phase 3, not deferred to some future unfunded project -- they just can't start until the catalog and classification underneath them are solid.

That gives us a fast, non-confrontational answer the moment a new request -- like merging duplicate records -- comes up mid-build.

lessons.title: Choosing the Stack: Microsoft Purview, Not Just a Spreadsheet of Data Owners
lessons.summary: The first architecture decision: why a shared spreadsheet of data owners cannot do what Veridian actually needs, and why Microsoft Purview's Data Map, glossary, and classification engine are the right foundation instead.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With V1 scoped, this is the first real architecture decision: what platform actually runs this governance program. The tempting, cheapest-looking answer is the one most organizations try first -- a shared spreadsheet or SharePoint list naming a data owner for each system, maybe a tab for sensitive columns. This video explains, in detail, why that approach cannot deliver any of the four V1 requirements at Veridian's actual scale, and why the right answer instead is Microsoft Purview: a single governance domain, Veridian Data Governance, that registers and scans all five production systems, hosts the business glossary, applies classification labels, and captures lineage across them.

This isn't a decision to rebuild or migrate anything Veridian already runs. Azure SQL, Salesforce, Oracle Financials, Snowflake, and the Fabric lakehouse all stay exactly where they are, doing exactly what they already do. Purview is the layer that gets added on top to make all five of them discoverable, owned, classified, and traceable from one place -- which is precisely what a spreadsheet, by its nature, cannot stay.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a library with five separate storage rooms, each run by a different librarian who never talks to the others, and no card catalog anywhere. One fix someone might suggest is a notebook where a volunteer writes down book titles by hand. That notebook is out of date the moment a new book arrives, nobody reliably updates it, and it definitely can't tell you which books have someone's private information printed inside the cover.

The better fix is an actual library system: one that automatically walks every shelf in every room, keeps the catalog current on its own, and puts a special lock-and-label on any book that needs one. That automatic, always-current, label-aware system is what Microsoft Purview gives Veridian -- something a hand-updated spreadsheet of data owners was never going to keep up with.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A spreadsheet of data owners would technically satisfy the ownership requirement for about as long as it takes for someone to leave the company, a system to get a new table added to it, or a well-meaning analyst to just not check the spreadsheet before writing a query against raw data -- which is close to the exact failure mode that produced three conflicting Active Customer numbers in the first place. The deeper problem at Veridian isn't that nobody has ever written down an owner's name; it's that there's never been a single, automatically maintained, discoverable system that five independently-run teams are structurally incentivized to actually keep using.

That's why the right fix is a platform purpose-built for this job, not a better document. Azure SQL, Salesforce, Oracle Financials, Snowflake, and Fabric all stay exactly as they are -- untouched, in production, doing their existing jobs -- because migrating or restructuring five live systems that Veridian's divisions depend on daily is both out of scope and unnecessarily risky. On top of them, Microsoft Purview provides the three things a spreadsheet structurally cannot: a Data Map that connects to and scans each system directly, so the inventory of critical data elements stays current without anyone manually re-typing it; Information Protection sensitivity labels, like Confidential – PII, that are actually attached to a column and can drive real access policy, not just a note in a spreadsheet cell; and a lineage capability that stitches together the hop from a source system through the Fabric semantic model into a Power BI dashboard, which is exactly the trail Grace's audit question requires and no spreadsheet, and no single tool's own internal lineage view, can see across all five systems at once.

The organizing container for all of this is one governance domain, Veridian Data Governance, created in Purview's Unified Catalog. Every glossary term, every classification label, every registered source, and every ownership assignment for this program lives inside that one domain -- which is the structural answer to who owns this, and where would I even look to find out, for every one of the five systems, going forward.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- List the actual constraints before naming a single tool

```
CONSTRAINTS:
  - All five systems (veridian-sql-prod, Salesforce, ORACLE_FIN,
    VERIDIAN_DW, Fabric lakehouse) are live production systems
    across three divisions and must stay untouched and read-only
    from the governance tooling's perspective
  - ~2.1 million customer identities across five systems -- manual
    tagging of ownership or classification does not scale and will
    not stay current
  - The root cause was the absence of any single, discoverable
    source of ownership, definitions, and classification -- whatever
    we choose has to be automatically maintained, not just
    accurate on the day someone fills it in
  - The audit requirement is cross-system by nature -- "everywhere a
    SSN is stored" cannot be answered by any one system's own
    internal metadata view
```

## Step 2 -- Assign one layer per responsibility

```
LAYER                  TOOL              RESPONSIBLE FOR
Governance domain /     Purview Unified    One organizing container,
  catalog               Catalog            "Veridian Data
                                            Governance" -- glossary,
                                            CDE inventory, ownership
Source scanning /       Purview Data Map   Registering and scanning
  metadata                                 veridian-sql-prod,
                                            Salesforce, ORACLE_FIN,
                                            VERIDIAN_DW, Fabric
Classification          Purview            Confidential – PII labels
                        Information        applied directly to
                        Protection          sensitive columns
Business glossary       Purview glossary   Active Customer, Engaged
                        terms              Account, and other
                                           governed definitions
Lineage                 Purview lineage    Source -> ETL/ELT -> Fabric
                                           lakehouse -> semantic
                                           model -> Power BI dashboard
Reporting / consumption Power BI           Unchanged -- still where
                                           Finance, Marketing, and
                                           executives read numbers
```

## Step 3 -- Name the alternatives seriously considered, and why they lose

```
- A shared spreadsheet/SharePoint list of data owners: rejected.
  This is close to what Veridian has informally tried already --
  it goes stale the first time a system changes, has no scanning
  capability, and cannot apply a classification label that actually
  does anything.
- Tagging ownership and sensitivity manually inside each of the five
  systems separately: rejected. Five times the work, five
  inconsistent formats, and still no single place to answer show
  me everywhere for an audit.
- Relying on Power BI's or Fabric's own built-in lineage view alone:
  rejected. It only sees as far back as Fabric -- it's blind to
  Oracle Financials, Salesforce, and veridian-sql-prod, and won't
  satisfy a lineage requirement that has to reach all the way to
  the original source.
```

## Step 4 -- Write the one-paragraph justification you'll reuse later

```
"We're not changing anything about how Azure SQL, Salesforce, Oracle
Financials, Snowflake, or Fabric already run. We're adding Microsoft
Purview as a governance layer on top -- one domain, Veridian Data
Governance, with all five systems registered and scanned in its Data
Map, so ownership, definitions, classification, and lineage all live
in exactly one place instead of five private spreadsheets nobody
keeps current."
```

## Step 5 -- Write down what this choice does NOT require

```
THIS DECISION DOES NOT REQUIRE:
  - Migrating any of the five source systems
  - Any downtime on Azure SQL, Oracle Financials, or Salesforce
  - Rebuilding the existing Power BI reports
  - Manually re-tagging every column by hand, system by system --
    Purview's scanning does the heavy lifting the spreadsheet
    approach never could
```

Saying plainly what this architecture does not touch is often what actually gets a cautious division leader to approve it -- the real objection behind do we need a whole new platform is almost always about risk to systems that already work, not cost, and naming that boundary directly answers it.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Chose Microsoft Purview over a spreadsheet-based approach: one governance domain, Veridian Data Governance, with all five production systems registered and scanned through the Data Map, classification handled by Information Protection labels, and lineage stitched from source through Fabric into Power BI. None of the five source systems change -- Purview is a layer added on top, not a migration.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We're not touching any system that already runs the business -- we're adding one governance platform that all five teams can discover and use, instead of five private spreadsheets that go stale the moment something changes. This also directly answers the kind of audit question that triggered this whole program.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We're not putting your billing, CRM, or financial systems at risk, and nothing visible changes for the teams using them today. We're adding one place where ownership, definitions, and sensitive-data classification live for all five systems at once, so the next audit question gets a complete answer instead of an estimate.

lessons.title: Designing the Governance Domain and Data Ownership Model
lessons.summary: Whiteboarding the Purview governance domain, a collection per division, and a real business-owner/technical-steward ownership model — before a single source gets registered.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Scope is locked, and Microsoft Purview is the chosen stack. Before anything gets registered in Purview's Data Map, this lesson whiteboards the shape the whole governance program hangs on: one governance domain, `Veridian Data Governance`, with a collection for each of Veridian Holdings' three divisions — Retail, Logistics, and Financial Services — and a real ownership model assigned to each one.

This is the architecture-planning lesson that matters most for everything downstream. Every scan Veridian runs starting in Lesson 8, every glossary term it approves, every sensitivity label it applies, lands inside the structure drawn here. Get the ownership model wrong, or skip assigning it until after the first scan, and Veridian ends up exactly where it started: a catalog full of data nobody is accountable for.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a big apartment building with three floors, and nobody has ever written down who's in charge of fixing things on each floor. When a pipe bursts, three different people show up, argue about whose job it was, and nothing gets fixed quickly. The smart fix is to assign one named person per floor *before* anything breaks — not after.

That's what we're doing here, except the "floors" are Veridian's three business divisions, and the "pipes" are their data. We're drawing the floor plan and writing down exactly whose name goes on each floor, before we even walk through the building to see what's there.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the structural decision every later Purview lesson depends on: a single governance domain containing one collection per business division, with two distinct ownership roles — business owner and technical steward — assigned at the collection level before any source registration happens. A governance domain is Purview's container for the glossary terms, data products, and classification policy a program owns; collections are the hierarchical containers inside it that scans, access rights, and ownership assignments all inherit from.

Veridian doesn't need three domains for three divisions, because Finance, Marketing, and the warehouse team all reason about overlapping concepts — the same customers, the same transactions — that a split-domain model would only fragment further. One domain, three collections, gets the division-level separation right without losing the shared vocabulary a single customer record needs. The ownership split matters just as much: a business owner is accountable for what the data means and who gets to use it; a technical steward is accountable for the data's structure, quality, and the scan that discovers it. Assigning both roles to a collection before it holds a single registered source is what turns a scan result into an accountable catalog entry instead of an orphaned one.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Draw the domain shape before opening the Purview portal

Whiteboard this the same way a warehouse project whiteboards a star schema before opening SSMS. At the top sits one governance domain: `Veridian Data Governance`. A governance domain in Purview is the container for everything the program owns — its glossary, its data products, its classification policy, and the collections nested beneath it. Veridian gets one domain, not three, because Finance, Marketing, and the warehouse team all reason about the same underlying concepts (the same customers, the same transactions); splitting the domain by division would only fragment a vocabulary that needs to stay shared.

## Step 2 — One collection per division, not one collection per source system

Inside `Veridian Data Governance`, create three top-level collections: `Retail`, `Logistics`, and `Financial Services` — mirroring Veridian's actual business divisions, not its technology inventory. Each division's registered sources will nest under its collection: `Financial Services` will hold `ORACLE_FIN`; `Retail` and `Logistics` will hold the relevant slices of `veridian-sql-prod`, Salesforce, `VERIDIAN_DW`, and the Fabric lakehouse, split by which division actually owns that data. Collections matter because Purview's access model and role assignments both inherit downward from them — granting Data Curator rights on the `Financial Services` collection lets someone manage every asset registered under it without touching Retail's or Logistics' data at all.

## Step 3 — Define two distinct ownership roles, not one blurry "owner"

Veridian's core problem was never a lack of capable people — it was that nobody could say, with a straight face, who was accountable for the customer data living in any given system. Fix that with two separate, named roles on every collection:

- **Business owner** — accountable for what the data *means* and how it's used. Approves glossary definitions, approves access requests, and is the first person a compliance auditor calls.
- **Technical steward** — accountable for the data's structure, quality, and the scan configuration itself. Fixes a broken scan, investigates a classification result that looks wrong, keeps the registered source's metadata current.

These are deliberately different people in most cases. A Financial Services business owner understands what "customer" means to Finance; a technical steward understands how `ORACLE_FIN` is actually built. Neither role alone is sufficient.

## Step 4 — Assign ownership before a single scan runs

This is the sequencing decision that matters most: ownership gets assigned to each collection *before* `veridian-sql-prod`, Salesforce, `ORACLE_FIN`, `VERIDIAN_DW`, or the Fabric lakehouse get registered in Lesson 8. Run a scan first, and Purview's Data Map fills with newly discovered assets that have no accountable name attached — an orphaned catalog entry nobody feels responsible for classifying or correcting. Assign business owner and technical steward at the collection level first, so every asset a scan later discovers inherits an owner the moment it lands.

## Step 5 — Decide how sub-collections will mirror each division's actual source footprint

A division's collection isn't a single flat bucket — it needs enough internal structure that a future scan result lands somewhere specific, not just somewhere divisional. Plan one sub-collection per registered source underneath each division collection: Financial Services / ORACLE_FIN, Retail / veridian-sql-prod, Retail / Salesforce, Logistics / veridian-sql-prod, and a shared cross-division sub-collection for VERIDIAN_DW and the Fabric lakehouse, since both blend data from more than one division and don't belong fully to either one. Sketching this now means Lesson 8's registration step is just filling in a structure that already exists, not inventing one under time pressure while a scan is queued and waiting.

## Step 6 — Write the ownership roster as a real artifact

Before Lesson 8, produce one table: collection, sub-collection, business owner, technical steward, for Retail, Logistics, and Financial Services, plus the shared warehouse/BI sub-collection. This roster is the first thing a compliance auditor will ask for, and it is the artifact every later lesson — the glossary approval workflow, the classification review, the scan results themselves — traces back to. Share it with all three division leads and get an explicit confirmation on each name before Lesson 8 begins; a roster nobody has actually agreed to is just as unaccountable as no roster at all.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Whiteboarded one governance domain, Veridian Data Governance, with a collection per division — Retail, Logistics, Financial Services — before registering a single source. Each collection gets a named business owner and a named technical steward assigned now, deliberately before any scan runs, so every asset Purview discovers in Lesson 8 lands with an accountable owner instead of as an orphaned catalog entry.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've designed the organizational structure the catalog will live in, and more importantly, we've named who's accountable for each division's data before we scan anything. That ownership roster is what lets us say, from day one, exactly who signs off on a definition or a classification question instead of it becoming a committee argument later.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Before we catalog a single piece of data, we're assigning a named owner to each business division's information — someone accountable for what it means, and someone accountable for its quality. That's the structural fix for the 'nobody owns this' problem you brought us in to solve, done before the technical work even starts.

lessons.title: Planning the Business Glossary and Critical Data Elements
lessons.summary: Building the critical data element inventory and resolving the real "Active Customer" conflict between Finance, Marketing, and the warehouse — before a single glossary term is published.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The ownership roster from Lesson 5 says who's accountable for each division's data. This lesson decides what that data actually *means* — starting with the one term everyone at Veridian Holdings uses constantly and defines differently: **Active Customer**. Finance's number comes from Oracle Financials. Marketing's comes from Salesforce. The warehouse team has its own blended number that disagrees with both. None of the three is simply wrong; each was built to answer a slightly different question, in isolation, years apart.

This video plans the business glossary and the critical data element (CDE) inventory it's built on — the small list of terms and fields important enough that Veridian cannot afford an ungoverned definition of them — and lays out the real process for turning three competing numbers into one approved definition inside Purview's glossary.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine three people in the same family each keeping their own calendar of "how many cousins we have," and each one counts differently — one includes cousins by marriage, one doesn't, one forgot to update after someone moved away. Nobody is lying; they just never sat down together and agreed on one rule for who counts as a cousin.

That's exactly what's happening with "Active Customer" at Veridian. Finance counts one way, Marketing counts another way, and the warehouse counts a third way. This lesson is about getting everyone in one room, writing down all three ways of counting, and agreeing on one official rule everyone will use from now on.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A business glossary is only as useful as the discipline behind which terms get governed and how conflicts between existing definitions get resolved — and the first discipline is scoping the glossary to critical data elements rather than trying to define every column in every system. A CDE is a term or field whose definition materially affects a regulatory report, a financial statement, or a cross-division decision; "Active Customer" qualifies immediately because Finance reports it to leadership, Marketing targets campaigns against it, and the warehouse blends it into executive dashboards — three different audiences making decisions off three different numbers for the same name.

Resolving it is not a matter of picking a side. It requires pulling each team's actual logic, naming precisely where the three definitions diverge — a customer Finance still counts as active because an invoice posted this quarter, a customer Marketing excludes because no campaign engagement occurred in 90 days, a customer the warehouse blends in because a Snowflake join picked up a stale Salesforce record — and negotiating one testable, written rule that all three teams sign off on before it's published as an approved Purview glossary term with assigned stewards and a defined status.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Build the critical data element inventory before drafting any definition

Not every field at Veridian needs glossary governance. Scope the first glossary pass to the terms whose definition materially changes a report, a regulatory filing, or a cross-division decision:

```
CANDIDATE CDEs (first pass):
  - Active Customer          (Finance, Marketing, warehouse all disagree)
  - Customer Lifetime Value   (depends entirely on Active Customer)
  - Net Revenue               (Financial Services, reconciliation-critical)
  - Customer Record of Record (which system wins when Oracle/Salesforce/
                                Snowflake disagree on the same person)
```

`Active Customer` goes first — everything else on this list is downstream of it.

## Step 2 — Pull each team's actual definition, in their own logic

```
Finance (ORACLE_FIN):     Any customer with a posted invoice in the
                          trailing 12 months — regardless of payment status.
Marketing (Salesforce):    Any contact with a logged campaign engagement
                          (open, click, event) in the trailing 90 days.
Warehouse (VERIDIAN_DW):   A blended view joining both source extracts,
                          currently inheriting whichever record landed
                          most recently in the nightly load — with no
                          agreed rule for which source wins on conflict.
```

## Step 3 — Name the real divergence out loud, with each owner in the room

The warehouse's number isn't a third opinion — it's an unintended side effect of a load order nobody designed on purpose. That distinction matters: Finance's and Marketing's definitions are each defensible; the warehouse's is a defect masquerading as a third definition, and it needs to be named as exactly that before the room tries to negotiate a compromise between three "equally valid" numbers.

## Step 4 — Negotiate one approved definition, not a vote

Draft a candidate rule and pressure-test it against real edge cases before anyone signs anything:

```
DRAFT: "Active Customer" = a customer with either a posted invoice in
the trailing 12 months (Finance's signal) OR a logged engagement in the
trailing 90 days (Marketing's signal) — counted once, keyed to a single
agreed customer-record-of-record, not whichever source landed last.
```

This resolves Finance's and Marketing's definitions by combining their signals rather than discarding either one, and it explicitly kills the warehouse's accidental "most recent load wins" behavior by requiring a deliberate record-of-record rule.

## Step 5 — Publish it as an approved term in Purview, with real metadata

In the Purview glossary, the term isn't just a sentence — it carries status (Draft to Approved), an assigned steward (the Financial Services business owner from Lesson 5, since Finance's data carries the most regulatory weight), related terms (Customer Lifetime Value, Net Revenue), and a linked example query stewards can run by hand to verify it:

```
TERM: Active Customer
STATUS: Approved
STEWARD: Financial Services business owner
EXPERTS: Marketing business owner, warehouse technical steward
RELATED TERMS: Customer Lifetime Value, Net Revenue, Customer Record of Record
VERIFICATION QUERY (run by hand against a sample month before sign-off):
  SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)
  FROM VERIDIAN_DW.CURATED.CUSTOMER_ACTIVITY
  WHERE invoice_posted_last_12mo = 1 OR engagement_last_90d = 1;
```

Only once Finance, Marketing, and the warehouse team have all signed off does the term move from Draft to Approved -- a status every later lesson's reporting can point back to.

## Step 6 — Fold the rest of the CDE inventory into the same workflow

Active Customer is the hardest term, not the only one. Customer Lifetime Value and Net Revenue both reference it directly, so neither can be drafted until Active Customer is Approved -- queue them as Draft with a dependency note now, and revisit once the foundational term is locked. Customer Record of Record gets drafted in parallel, since it's the rule (not a number) that decides which system wins when Oracle, Salesforce, and Snowflake disagree about the same person -- a rule the Active Customer definition already leans on in Step 4, which is worth stating explicitly rather than leaving implicit.

## Step 7 — Assign stewardship responsibility going forward, not just for this one approval

An approved term isn't finished the day it's published -- it needs an owner responsible for revisiting it if the underlying systems change (a new Salesforce campaign-engagement field, a new Oracle invoice status). Log that ongoing responsibility against the same business owner named as steward in Step 5, so a future schema change at any of the three source systems has a named person whose job it is to notice and ask whether the glossary term still holds.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Pulled the actual logic behind Finance's, Marketing's, and the warehouse's three Active Customer numbers. Finance and Marketing each had a defensible rule based on different signals; the warehouse's number turned out to be an unintended side effect of load order, not a real third definition. Drafted one combined rule, got sign-off from all three, and published it in Purview's glossary as Approved with the Financial Services owner assigned as steward.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We now have one written, signed-off definition of Active Customer replacing three competing ones, and we found that one of the three numbers wasn't actually a disagreement — it was a data defect nobody had flagged before. That's logged separately so it doesn't get mistaken for a matter of opinion the next time it comes up.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Finance, Marketing, and our warehouse team have agreed, in writing, on exactly what counts as an active customer. One of the three numbers we'd been reporting from turned out to be unintentional, not a legitimate second opinion — which means this fix removes a real source of confusion, not just a difference of taste.

lessons.title: Planning Data Classification and Sensitivity Labels
lessons.summary: Designing the sensitivity label taxonomy and the classification plan across all five systems — and committing to classify the real underlying tables, not just the views people normally query.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Build the sensitivity label taxonomy first, independent of any one system

Before looking at a single column in any of Veridian's five systems, define the label set everything will be measured against. Microsoft Purview Information Protection sensitivity labels form a hierarchy, and Veridian's needs exactly four:

```
Public              -- no restriction (marketing collateral, published rates)
Internal            -- Veridian-only, low individual risk (store schedules,
                        aggregate sales totals)
Confidential         -- sensitive but not individually identifying
                        (unaggregated financials, internal forecasts)
Confidential - PII   -- customer SSNs, account numbers, anything that
                        identifies a specific person financially
```

Each label maps to real handling rules — who can see it, whether it can leave Veridian's tenant, whether it can be exported to a Power BI export or a CSV — decided now, before any column gets tagged.

## Step 2 — Map suspected sensitive columns by division, before scanning confirms anything

This is a hypothesis to test in Lesson 8, not a finished answer:

```
Financial Services (ORACLE_FIN):  customer SSNs, bank account numbers,
                                   income figures -- highest suspected
                                   concentration of Confidential - PII
Retail (veridian-sql-prod,
  Salesforce):                    customer emails, phone numbers,
                                   loyalty account numbers -- mostly
                                   Confidential, some PII at the contact
                                   level
Logistics (veridian-sql-prod):    shipment and vendor data -- mostly
                                   Internal, low PII exposure
Warehouse/BI (VERIDIAN_DW,
  Fabric lakehouse, Power BI):     blended customer and financial data --
                                   inherits the highest label of anything
                                   feeding it, which likely means
                                   Confidential - PII once Financial
                                   Services data lands in it
```

## Step 3 — Commit, in writing, to classifying structure — not the view people happen to query

This is the single most important planning decision in this lesson. Every one of Veridian's five systems has at least one curated, cleaned-up reporting view that analysts actually run their day-to-day queries against — and every one of those views sits on top of a wider, messier base table that most people never look at directly. A classification plan that only scans the view a team is used to querying will classify exactly what that view exposes and nothing underneath it.

Write the rule down now, before a single scan runs: **classification scope includes the real underlying base tables and schemas registered for each source, not only the views or reporting layers a business team currently uses.** For `ORACLE_FIN` specifically, that means the scan scope needs to reach past whatever reporting schema the Financial Services team hands over by default and confirm it covers the actual base tables sitting underneath it — a decision to revisit explicitly once the registration conversation in Lesson 8 happens with Oracle's systems team.

## Step 4 — Decide label inheritance and the human-review checkpoint

Automated classification in Purview flags likely sensitive data using built-in classifiers (U.S. Social Security Number, credit card number, bank account number patterns), but a pattern match is a candidate, not a verdict. Decide the review rule now: any column automatically classified as PII gets its suggested label auto-applied, but any column a human steward believes *should* carry a label — based on its name or context — and didn't get flagged, goes into a manual review queue the technical steward checks weekly. Automated classification catches what matches a pattern; it does not catch a column named `cust_ssn_enc` if the data inside it doesn't look like a standard SSN format.

## Step 5 — Document the plan as an approval artifact, signed by each division's business owner

Before Lesson 8, the sensitivity label taxonomy, the suspected-column map, and the base-table classification commitment all go into one document, reviewed and signed by each division's business owner from Lesson 5. This is the artifact a compliance auditor will ask to see first if anything is ever later found unclassified.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine your family has four different colored folders for important papers: green for "anyone can see this," yellow for "just us," orange for "keep this quiet," and red for "this one has someone's actual personal information in it, be really careful." Before you sort a single paper, you'd agree on what goes in which folder.

That's what we're doing here — deciding the four colors (Public, Internal, Confidential, and Confidential-PII) before looking at any of Veridian's real data. And we're also making one important promise to ourselves: when we actually go looking for sensitive papers later, we're going to check the real filing cabinet, not just the neat summary folder someone keeps on top of the desk — because the messy real cabinet underneath is where the truly sensitive stuff might actually be sitting.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is classification policy design, and the two decisions that matter most are the taxonomy itself and the scope commitment. The taxonomy — Public, Internal, Confidential, Confidential-PII — needs to be small enough that a steward can apply it consistently and specific enough that each label maps to an actual handling rule, not just a color.

The scope commitment is the more consequential decision: classification is only as trustworthy as the structures it actually inspects, and every real system has a convenient, curated reporting layer sitting in front of a messier base-table reality most people never query directly. Committing now — on paper, before registration — to classify real underlying tables rather than whatever view a business team hands over by default is what keeps automated classification honest. A scan scoped to a reporting view will classify that view accurately and say nothing true about what's sitting one layer beneath it.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 6 resolved what "Active Customer" means. This lesson plans a different kind of governance decision: which data at Veridian Holdings is sensitive enough to need a Purview Information Protection sensitivity label, and exactly how classification will be scoped before a single scan touches `veridian-sql-prod`, Salesforce, `ORACLE_FIN`, `VERIDIAN_DW`, or the Fabric lakehouse.

We design the label taxonomy, map which systems and divisions are suspected to carry sensitive data like customer SSNs and financial details, and commit — on paper, now — to classifying the real underlying data structures rather than only the polished reporting views analysts are used to querying. That commitment is a planning decision this lesson makes deliberately; what it protects against is the subject of a much later lesson in this series.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Designed the sensitivity label taxonomy — Public, Internal, Confidential, Confidential-PII — and mapped suspected sensitive columns per division ahead of any scan. The decision I'm most insistent on: classification scope has to reach the real base tables for every registered source, not whatever curated reporting view a business team hands over by default. That's written into the plan now, before registration conversations start in the next lesson.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've agreed on the four-tier sensitivity labeling scheme and roughly where the highest-risk data is likely to live, division by division. We've also set a scoping rule for the classification scan itself — go after the real underlying tables, not just the summary views — which protects us from a classification pass that looks complete but quietly missed what's underneath.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've mapped out, in advance, roughly where your most sensitive customer and financial data is likely to be sitting across all five systems, and we've set the rule that our scans need to look at the real data structures, not just the tidy reports people are used to looking at. That's the planning step that keeps a classification effort from giving false confidence.

lessons.title: Registering and Scanning the Data Sources in Purview
lessons.summary: Registering all five Veridian data sources in Purview's Data Map, running the first scans, and reviewing automated classification against what still needs a human steward's review.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Planning is done. This is the first lesson where Microsoft Purview's Data Map actually gets used to register and scan Veridian Holdings' real systems: `veridian-sql-prod` (Azure SQL), Salesforce, `ORACLE_FIN` (Oracle Financials), `VERIDIAN_DW` (Snowflake), and the Fabric lakehouse feeding the executive Power BI dashboard. Each source registers under the collection its division owns, inheriting the business owner and technical steward assigned back in Lesson 5.

We run the first scans against each source, then review what Purview's built-in automated classification found on its own — and just as importantly, what it didn't find, and still needs a human steward's eyes before anyone trusts it.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine you just got five new filing cabinets delivered — one for each department — and before anyone can use them, you have to label each cabinet, tell the building who's allowed to open it, and then actually go through every drawer once to see what's really inside. That's what this lesson does: we officially register all five of Veridian's data systems in Purview, run the first real scan of each one, and then sit down and look at what the scan found — some of it the computer figured out on its own, and some of it a person still needs to double-check by hand.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the first implementation lesson in the series, and it's where the Lesson 5 ownership model and the Lesson 7 classification plan get tested against real metadata for the first time. Registering a source in Purview's Data Map means creating a data source object under the correct collection, authenticating a scan (via a managed identity or a registered application, depending on the source type), and defining a scan rule set that specifies which classifiers run and which system or custom classification rules apply.

`veridian-sql-prod`, Salesforce, `VERIDIAN_DW`, and the Fabric lakehouse each register cleanly against their full schemas. `ORACLE_FIN` registers through credentials the Oracle Financials systems team provisions, and the scan is scoped to the schema and views that team has set up for reporting access — the same reporting-oriented access path most of Finance's own analysts already use day to day. Once each scan completes, the review step matters as much as the scan itself: Purview's built-in classifiers reliably flag patterns like email addresses, phone numbers, and standard-format financial identifiers, but a classifier only flags what matches a known pattern — it says nothing about data it was never pointed at. That's why every scan result gets reviewed against the suspected-sensitive map from Lesson 7, not just accepted as complete on its own.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Register veridian-sql-prod (Azure SQL) under its division collections

In Purview's Data Map, register a new Azure SQL Database source: server name, database `veridian-sql-prod`, connecting via a managed identity granted `db_datareader` on the relevant schemas. Assign it to the `Retail` and `Logistics` collections, split by schema, so each schema's scanned assets inherit the correct business owner and technical steward from Lesson 5 automatically.

## Step 2 — Register Salesforce as a CRM source

Register Salesforce under the `Retail` collection, authenticating via a connected Salesforce integration user with read access to Accounts, Contacts, and Opportunities. Salesforce assets land in the catalog as objects rather than tables, but they follow the same collection-inheritance rule as every other source.

## Step 3 — Register ORACLE_FIN under Financial Services

Register `ORACLE_FIN` under the `Financial Services` collection, using credentials provisioned by Oracle's own systems team. The scan is scoped to the schema and reporting views that team provisions access to — the standard access path Finance's own analysts already use for day-to-day reporting. Confirm the scan rule set applies the same system classification rules (`U.S. Social Security Number`, `Credit Card Number`, `Bank Account Number`) that every other financial-adjacent source uses, so results are comparable across systems.

## Step 4 — Register VERIDIAN_DW and the Fabric lakehouse

Register the Snowflake warehouse `VERIDIAN_DW` under a shared collection reflecting its blended, cross-division nature, authenticating with a dedicated read-only Snowflake role. Register the Fabric lakehouse feeding the Power BI semantic model and executive dashboard the same way, scoped to the lakehouse's tables rather than only the semantic model sitting on top of it.

## Step 5 — Run the first scans and separate automated findings from what still needs review

Trigger an on-demand scan for each of the five sources. When they complete, build one findings table:

```
veridian-sql-prod:  Classifier flagged customer emails, phone numbers,
                    loyalty account numbers as Confidential-tier PII.
                    Matches Lesson 7's prediction closely.
Salesforce:         Classifier flagged contact emails and phone numbers.
                    No financial PII present, as expected for a CRM.
ORACLE_FIN:         Classifier flagged account numbers and GL codes as
                    Confidential. No U.S. Social Security Number matches
                    surfaced in this pass -- lower than Lesson 7's
                    prediction for this source, flagged for the
                    Financial Services technical steward to review
                    against what the registered schema actually covers.
VERIDIAN_DW:        Classifier flagged blended customer PII consistent
                    with everything feeding it from Retail and Logistics.
Fabric lakehouse:   Classifier flagged customer identifiers consistent
                    with the semantic model built on top of it.
```

Every row with a result that matches Lesson 7's prediction gets its labels accepted. The one row that came back lighter than expected — `ORACLE_FIN` showing no SSN matches against a source predicted to carry the highest PII concentration at Veridian — goes into the technical steward's manual review queue rather than being accepted as a clean result, exactly the kind of discrepancy the Lesson 7 review checkpoint exists to catch.

## Step 6 — Decide what happens next with what still needs review

A first scan is never the finish line. For every source whose result matched the Lesson 7 prediction, move its sensitivity labels from suggested to confirmed and let the technical steward's weekly review queue handle anything new that shows up on the next scan cycle. For ORACLE_FIN, the discrepancy goes on a short, dated follow-up list: confirm with the Oracle Financials systems team exactly which schema and views the registered scan actually covers, and whether the base tables beneath that reporting layer carry structure the scan never saw. Until that follow-up closes, ORACLE_FIN's classification status gets marked provisional rather than complete in the ownership roster from Lesson 5 — a distinction that matters, because a provisional status is a flag for someone to act on, while a complete status quietly invites everyone downstream to stop asking questions.

## Step 7 — Set the recurring scan schedule before moving on

A one-time scan only tells you what was true the day it ran. Configure each source's scan trigger to run on a recurring schedule — weekly for the faster-changing sources like Salesforce and veridian-sql-prod, monthly for ORACLE_FIN and VERIDIAN_DW where schema changes are rarer but still happen — so new columns, new tables, and new sensitive fields get caught automatically going forward rather than depending on someone remembering to re-run a scan by hand. Each scheduled run writes its results to the same Data Map assets scanned here, so classification history becomes visible over time instead of resetting with every scan.

Four of the five came back matching what we predicted in Lesson 7. ORACLE_FIN came back lighter on PII than expected for a source we'd flagged as the highest-risk one at Veridian — no SSN pattern matches in this pass — so that's going into the technical steward's review queue rather than getting signed off as clean.

One source came back with fewer sensitive-data flags than we expected going in, and rather than assume that's good news, we've logged it for a follow-up review before anyone relies on that result.
