One result came back lighter than we expected on the financial side, so we're following up before treating that as the final word — we'd rather double-check now than be surprised later.

lessons.title: Building the Business Glossary and Resolving the Revenue Definition Conflict
lessons.summary: Finance's Oracle count, Marketing's Salesforce count, and the warehouse's blended count all disagree on 'Active Customer' -- this lesson resolves it as one approved Purview glossary term, linked to the real columns.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: With all five Veridian Holdings sources registered and scanned in Purview, the catalog knows that "Active Customer" exists as a concept -- Finance's Oracle extract, Marketing's Salesforce reports, and the Snowflake warehouse's own blended calculation all use the phrase, and all three disagree. This lesson builds the fix: formally publishing Daniel's Oracle billing-basis number as the one approved Active Customer term in the Purview Business Glossary, giving Lena's Salesforce number its own governed name -- Engaged Account -- instead of forcing it into a fight it was never going to win, and retiring the warehouse's undocumented blend now that the other two are properly named and owned. By the end, "Active Customer" means exactly one thing at Veridian, sourced from exactly one system, and Purview can prove it.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine three friends each keeping score of how many people came to a lemonade stand, but each friend counts differently -- one only counts people who paid cash, one counts anyone who said hi, one counts people from last month too. They'd all get different numbers and argue about who's right. This lesson is about getting all three friends in a room, agreeing on one clear rule for what counts as a customer, writing that rule down in one place everyone can check, and then going back and relabeling each friend's scorecard so they all follow the same rule.
lessons.explainProfessional: This is business glossary governance in Microsoft Purview, and the deliverable is two terms, not one document -- governed glossary terms in the Veridian Data Governance domain that each carry a formal definition, an approval record, a named owner, and asset links, all queryable and auditable inside the catalog rather than living in someone's slide deck. The hard part isn't the Purview mechanics; it's resolving the actual conflict without declaring anyone's number simply wrong. Finance's Oracle-based count reflects real billing activity the board already trusts; Marketing's Salesforce count reflects a genuinely different signal, CRM engagement; the warehouse's blended number is an undocumented average of both that nobody can actually defend. The resolution that holds up: let Active Customer mean exactly what Finance has always meant by it -- now formally governed and single-sourced from ORACLE_FIN -- and give Marketing's number its own name and its own equally real governance, rather than forcing two legitimate but different signals into one blended, undocumented number nobody can stand behind in an audit.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Document the three competing numbers before touching the glossary

Before writing a definition, prove the conflict is real with numbers, not assertions. Pull each division's current count:

```sql
-- Finance's number (Oracle Financials -- open AR / recent invoice activity)
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT CUSTOMER_ID) AS finance_active_count
FROM ORACLE_FIN.VW_CUSTOMER_SUMMARY
WHERE OPEN_BALANCE > 0
   OR LAST_INVOICE_DATE >= ADD_MONTHS(SYSDATE, -12);

-- Marketing's number (Salesforce -- CRM engagement)
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT Id) AS marketing_active_count
FROM SALESFORCE.CONTACT
WHERE Status__c = 'Customer'
  AND LastActivityDate >= DATEADD(day, -90, CURRENT_DATE);

-- The warehouse's own blended number (VERIDIAN_DW -- undocumented legacy rule)
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT CUSTOMER_KEY) AS warehouse_active_count
FROM VERIDIAN_DW.DIM_CUSTOMER
WHERE ACTIVE_FLAG = 'Y';
```

Three queries, three different counts, none reconciling -- and critically, none of the three divisions is "wrong." They're each answering a legitimate but different question.

## Step 2 — Run a definition resolution session and write the rule down

Bring together Finance's Daniel Reyes, Marketing's Lena Fitzgerald, the warehouse/DW lead Victor Kessler, and the Data Governance Council under the Veridian Data Governance domain. The real resolution, reached by recognizing Finance and Marketing were never actually measuring the same thing:

> **Active Customer**: a customer with at least one completed, non-voided, non-fully-refunded invoice in Oracle Financials within the trailing 12 months -- Finance's existing billing-basis definition, now formally governed rather than just informally trusted.
>
> **Engaged Account**: a separate, equally governed term for Marketing's existing metric -- a contact with CRM engagement activity within the trailing 90 days. Not a lesser or rejected version of Active Customer; a genuinely different, useful signal with its own name.

The warehouse's blended number, once its undocumented join logic was examined, turns out to answer a question nobody actually needs answered once the other two are properly named and owned -- it gets retired, not replaced.

## Step 3 — Create the governed terms in the Purview Business Glossary

In the Veridian Data Governance governance domain, create two new Business Glossary terms:

**Active Customer**
- Definition: the exact sentence from Step 2
- Status: Approved
- Owner: Daniel Reyes, Finance
- Authoritative source: ORACLE_FIN only -- this term is intentionally single-sourced, not blended

**Engaged Account**
- Definition: the exact sentence from Step 2
- Status: Approved
- Owner: Lena Fitzgerald, Marketing
- Authoritative source: Salesforce only

## Step 4 — Attach the approval record

Add the sign-off as a resource link on the term: names and titles of the Finance, Marketing, and Data Governance Council representatives, the approval date, and a short note on what each division's prior definition was and why it changed. This is what makes the term defensible later, not just agreed-upon in a meeting nobody wrote down.

## Step 5 — Link each term to its one authoritative column, and retire the rest

In the Purview Data Catalog:

- ORACLE_FIN.VW_CUSTOMER_SUMMARY → `CUSTOMER_STATUS` gets the **Active Customer** business term -- the only column that does.
- Salesforce → `Contact.Status__c` gets the **Engaged Account** business term.
- veridian-sql-prod → `dbo.Customers.IsActiveFlag` is reviewed and found to be an internal operational flag that was never actually governed by either definition -- flagged for its own follow-up, not forced to conform to either term today.
- VERIDIAN_DW → `DIM_CUSTOMER.ACTIVE_FLAG`, the undocumented blended calculation, is marked deprecated in the catalog with a note pointing to Active Customer and Engaged Account as its replacements.

A business term intentionally attached to exactly one column, not scattered across four systems that each computed something different, is what makes "Active Customer" mean one thing going forward instead of a label four systems each interpret their own way.

## Step 6 — Confirm both terms produce one stable number each

Active Customer now comes from exactly one place -- ORACLE_FIN -- so there's nothing left to reconcile for it; it was always Finance's real number, just newly governed. Engaged Account is the same story for Salesforce. The confirmation that matters here is organizational, not technical: with `VERIDIAN_DW.DIM_CUSTOMER.ACTIVE_FLAG` deprecated, the next person who goes looking for "the active customer number" finds the governed term and its one real source, not a third competing calculation.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Resolved the Active Customer conflict by recognizing Finance and Marketing were never measuring the same thing: published Finance's Oracle billing-basis number as the one approved Active Customer term, single-sourced from ORACLE_FIN.VW_CUSTOMER_SUMMARY, and gave Marketing's Salesforce number its own governed term -- Engaged Account. Retired the warehouse's undocumented blended flag and linked each new term to exactly one real column -- not scattered across four systems the way the old approach would have.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Finance, Marketing, and the warehouse team have been reporting three different 'active customer' counts for years. We got all three in a room, agreed on one rule, and that rule is now published and linked to the real data in Purview -- so every future report pulls from the same definition instead of each team's own interpretation.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Your three teams have been quoting different active-customer numbers in the same meetings for years, and none of them were technically wrong -- they were just answering different questions. We fixed that by agreeing on one rule, writing it down formally, and wiring it directly into the data so it's enforced automatically, not just recommended.

lessons.title: Assigning Data Owners and Stewards
lessons.summary: A named RACI matrix -- business owner plus technical steward for Customer, Financial, and Product/Inventory -- entered directly as Purview Data Owner and Expert assignments.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: The Active Customer glossary term from the last lesson has an approval record, but approval records fade without a name attached to defend them. This lesson assigns real ownership: a RACI-style matrix naming a business owner and a technical steward for each of Veridian's three major data domains -- Customer, Financial, and Product/Inventory -- and then enters those exact names as Data Owner and Data Expert contacts on the registered Purview sources and glossary terms those domains cover. Ownership that only exists in a spreadsheet isn't governance; ownership entered into the catalog, next to the asset itself, is.
lessons.explainSimple: Think about a school where every locker has a name on it, so if something goes wrong -- a locker's stuck, something's missing -- everyone knows exactly who to ask. Right now, a lot of Veridian's data is like a hallway of lockers with no names on them: nobody officially owns the customer list, or the financial numbers, or the inventory numbers, so when something's wrong, nobody knows who's supposed to fix it. This lesson puts a real name on every locker.
lessons.explainProfessional: This is data ownership assignment, and the governance mechanism that makes it real in Purview is the Contacts section on a registered data source or glossary term: an Owner field for business accountability and an Expert field for technical stewardship. The distinction matters because they answer different questions when something breaks -- the business owner can say whether a number is wrong because the business rule changed, the technical steward can say whether it's wrong because a pipeline failed. A RACI matrix is the planning artifact that gets you to those two names per domain, deliberately; naming one person 'responsible for everything' just recreates the single-point-of-failure problem governance is supposed to solve. Entering those names directly on the asset -- not just in an org chart slide -- is what lets anyone in the catalog, three divisions and one domain away from the person who assigned it, find exactly who to ask without a hallway conversation.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Identify the domains that actually need owners

Rather than assigning ownership asset-by-asset, group Veridian's registered sources into the three domains that reflect how the business actually thinks about its data:

```
Customer domain:    veridian-sql-prod (dbo.Customers), Salesforce,
                    VERIDIAN_DW.DIM_CUSTOMER, "Engaged Account" glossary term
Financial domain:   ORACLE_FIN (GL, AP, AR, VW_CUSTOMER_SUMMARY),
                    VERIDIAN_DW revenue fact tables, "Active Customer"
                    glossary term
Product/Inventory:  Fabric lakehouse inventory tables, Power BI semantic
                    model, VERIDIAN_DW inventory fact tables
```

## Step 2 — Build the RACI matrix with named people, not roles

```
DOMAIN              BUSINESS OWNER (A)              TECHNICAL STEWARD (R)
Customer            Priya Nair                      Marcus Webb
                    VP, Customer Experience          Senior DBA, veridian-sql-prod
                                                      & Salesforce integration
Financial           David Chen                      Elena Petrov
                    Corporate Controller             Oracle Financials DBA
Product/Inventory   Raj Thakur                      Sam Ortiz
                    VP, Supply Chain                 Fabric Lakehouse Engineer
```

The business owner is Accountable for what the data should mean and who can see it; the technical steward is Responsible for the pipeline, schema, and scan health that keep it correct day to day. Marketing and the Data Governance Council are Consulted on the Customer domain given the glossary work from Lesson 9; all three domain owners are Informed of any sensitivity-label or lineage change (Lessons 11 and 12).

## Step 3 — Enter owners and stewards on each registered source in Purview

Open each source's asset page under the Veridian Data Governance domain's Data Map and update the Contacts tab:

- veridian-sql-prod → Owner: Priya Nair · Expert: Marcus Webb
- Salesforce → Owner: Priya Nair · Expert: Marcus Webb
- ORACLE_FIN → Owner: David Chen · Expert: Elena Petrov
- VERIDIAN_DW → split by table group: customer tables to Priya Nair/Marcus Webb, financial fact tables to David Chen/Elena Petrov, inventory fact tables to Raj Thakur/Sam Ortiz
- Fabric lakehouse + Power BI semantic model → Owner: Raj Thakur · Expert: Sam Ortiz

## Step 4 — Assign ownership on the glossary term itself, not just the tables

Update both glossary terms from Lesson 9 the same way: "Active Customer" with Owner: David Chen, Expert: Elena Petrov, since it's single-sourced from ORACLE_FIN and sits in the Financial domain; "Engaged Account" with Owner: Priya Nair, Expert: Marcus Webb, since it's single-sourced from Salesforce and sits in the Customer domain. Either way, a question about a definition routes to a named person instead of landing in the Data Governance Council's general inbox.

## Step 5 — Audit for coverage gaps before calling this done

```sql
SELECT asset_name, domain, business_owner, technical_steward
FROM VERIDIAN_DW.GOVERNANCE.vw_purview_ownership_export
WHERE business_owner IS NULL OR technical_steward IS NULL;
```

Run this against the governance export view after entering contacts and confirm it returns zero rows for every asset registered in Lesson 8 -- an unowned asset is exactly the kind of gap that's invisible until the day someone needs an answer and can't find one.

## Step 6 — Set a review cadence

Document a quarterly ownership review in the domain's governance documentation: owners confirm they're still accurate, and any organizational change (a promotion, a reorg) triggers an update to the Contacts tab the same week, not whenever someone happens to notice it's stale.

## Step 7 — Test the matrix against a real question, not a hypothetical one

Ownership only matters if it resolves a real question faster than before. Walk through one concretely: "Oracle just changed how VW_CUSTOMER_SUMMARY.CUSTOMER_STATUS gets computed upstream -- whose backlog does confirming it still matches the Lesson 9 definition go on?" Checking the RACI matrix gives an immediate answer: Elena Petrov (technical steward, Financial domain) owns the check, David Chen (business owner) signs off that the column still matches the approved definition, and Priya Nair is Informed because Customer Experience reporting references the same term. Before this matrix existed, that question would have bounced between three inboxes for a week.

## Step 8 — Record the escalation path for disputes

Document what happens when a business owner and a technical steward disagree -- for example, if Marcus Webb says a schema change is needed but Priya Nair worries it breaks a downstream Salesforce sync. The escalation path routes to the Data Governance Council under the Veridian Data Governance domain, with a decision logged against the affected asset, so the resolution itself becomes part of that asset's auditable history rather than a conversation nobody wrote down.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built the ownership RACI across our three domains -- Customer, Financial, Product/Inventory -- and entered named business owners and technical stewards directly on the Purview Contacts tab for every registered source and on the Active Customer glossary term itself. Ran the ownership export audit query and confirmed zero gaps across everything registered in Lesson 8.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Every major data domain now has one named business decision-maker and one named technical contact, entered directly into the catalog rather than sitting in a slide somewhere. That means any question about a dataset -- is this number right, who approved this definition -- has a specific person to go to instead of a group email.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've put a name on every major piece of your data -- who's accountable for what it means, and who's responsible for keeping it technically correct. That's the difference between data governance being a policy on paper and actually being enforceable when something needs an answer fast.

lessons.title: Applying Sensitivity Labels Across Systems
lessons.summary: Confidential – PII labels applied across every column Purview's scanners flagged in veridian-sql-prod, Salesforce, and VERIDIAN_DW, with a clean, fully-reviewed pass on ORACLE_FIN.VW_CUSTOMER_SUMMARY.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: With owners assigned, this lesson applies Microsoft Purview Information Protection sensitivity labels -- Confidential – PII and related labels -- across every source scanned in Lesson 8: veridian-sql-prod, Salesforce, VERIDIAN_DW, and ORACLE_FIN.VW_CUSTOMER_SUMMARY. The goal is thorough, correct classification of everything that was actually registered and scanned, so that any system touching customer PII carries a visible label that downstream policies -- access reviews, DLP rules, Fabric and Power BI inheritance -- can act on automatically.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine putting a red sticker on every box in a warehouse that has something private inside, like someone's address or ID number, so that anyone handling the boxes knows to be careful with the red ones and can move the others around freely. This lesson is about walking through every box that's actually inside the warehouse and putting that red sticker on the right ones -- carefully checking each box that's really there.
lessons.explainProfessional: This is Microsoft Purview Information Protection sensitivity labeling, and the discipline is thoroughness against what Purview's classifiers actually found in the scanned content -- not a gut-feel pass. Each of the four scanned sources gets reviewed against its classification results (built-in classifiers like U.S. Social Security Number, Email Address, Phone Number) and labeled accordingly: Confidential – PII on any column carrying a detected PII pattern, a lighter internal-use label on everything else. Labels applied at the column level in Purview propagate downstream through lineage-aware inheritance into Fabric and Power BI artifacts that reference those columns, which is what makes labeling worth doing at the source rather than re-labeling every downstream report by hand. The work here is scoped precisely to what was registered and scanned in Lesson 8 -- a classification program is only ever as complete as its inventory, and the confirmation step at the end of this lesson is to verify every column across that inventory has a deliberate label, correct or confirmed non-sensitive, with none left unreviewed.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Confirm the label taxonomy before labeling anything

The Veridian Data Governance domain uses four Purview Information Protection labels: Public, Internal, Confidential – Financial, and Confidential – PII. This lesson applies Confidential – PII wherever Purview's classification scan detected a PII pattern, across the sources registered in Lesson 8.

## Step 2 — Review classification results for veridian-sql-prod

Purview's scan flagged `dbo.Customers.SSN` (U.S. Social Security Number), `dbo.Customers.Email` (Email Address), `dbo.Customers.Phone` (Phone Number), and `dbo.Customers.DateOfBirth` (Date of Birth). Apply Confidential – PII to all four columns. `dbo.Customers.CustomerID` and `dbo.Customers.Region` carry no detected pattern and stay Internal.

## Step 3 — Review classification results for Salesforce

The scan flagged `Contact.Email`, `Contact.Phone`, and `Contact.MailingAddress`. Apply Confidential – PII to all three. `Contact.Status__c` and `Contact.LastActivityDate` stay Internal.

## Step 4 — Review classification results for VERIDIAN_DW

`DIM_CUSTOMER` carries blended attributes sourced from upstream systems, including `Email` and `Phone` columns populated during the warehouse load. Apply Confidential – PII to both. Revenue and inventory fact tables (`FACT_SALES`, inventory facts) contain no PII patterns and stay Internal.

## Step 5 — Review classification results for ORACLE_FIN.VW_CUSTOMER_SUMMARY

Walk every column the scan returned: `CUSTOMER_ID`, `CUSTOMER_NAME`, `OPEN_BALANCE`, `LAST_INVOICE_DATE`, `CUSTOMER_STATUS`. None triggered a PII classifier. That's a clean result: this view was built specifically for finance reporting, and nothing in it needs a Confidential – PII label. Mark it Internal and move on; there's nothing further to flag here.

## Step 6 — Confirm label inheritance into Fabric and Power BI

Spot-check that the Confidential – PII label on `VERIDIAN_DW.DIM_CUSTOMER.Email` propagates into the Fabric lakehouse table referencing it and into the Power BI semantic model's corresponding field -- Purview's lineage-aware label inheritance should carry it automatically, without a separate manual labeling pass downstream.

## Step 7 — Audit for unlabeled columns across everything in scope

```sql
SELECT source_name, schema_name, table_name, column_name
FROM VERIDIAN_DW.GOVERNANCE.vw_purview_classification_export
WHERE sensitivity_label IS NULL
  AND source_name IN ('veridian-sql-prod', 'Salesforce', 'VERIDIAN_DW', 'ORACLE_FIN');
```

Run this against the governance export view and confirm zero rows -- every column across the four sources registered and scanned in Lesson 8 now carries a deliberate label, whether that's Confidential – PII or a confirmed Internal. Nothing is left unreviewed.

## Step 8 — Document the labeling pass

Record the labeling date, the classifier results reviewed, and the resulting label counts per source in the domain's governance log, so the next access review or audit has a dated record of what was labeled and on what basis.

## Step 9 — Connect labels to enforcement, not just visibility

A sensitivity label by itself is a tag; it becomes a control once a policy reads it. Confirm that Microsoft Purview Information Protection's auto-labeling and Data Loss Prevention policies for Confidential – PII are scoped to the Veridian Data Governance domain's registered assets, so that a Confidential – PII column -- `dbo.Customers.SSN`, `Contact.Email`, `DIM_CUSTOMER.Email` -- triggers the organization's existing DLP rules (blocking an unencrypted export, for example) the same way it would if someone had hand-labeled a document. Labeling without this step leaves the catalog accurate but toothless.

## Step 10 — Set the re-scan cadence

Schedule the four sources' Purview scans to re-run on the same cadence as their data refresh (nightly for veridian-sql-prod and Salesforce, aligned with the warehouse load for VERIDIAN_DW and ORACLE_FIN), so a newly added column -- a future schema change on any of these four systems -- gets classified and labeled automatically on its next scan instead of silently going unreviewed until someone happens to notice it.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Applied Confidential – PII labels across every column Purview's scanners flagged in veridian-sql-prod, Salesforce, and VERIDIAN_DW -- SSN, email, phone, date of birth, and the warehouse's blended contact fields. Reviewed ORACLE_FIN.VW_CUSTOMER_SUMMARY column by column; the scan found no PII patterns in it, which lines up with it being a finance reporting view, so it's labeled Internal with nothing further to flag. Ran the classification export audit and confirmed zero unlabeled columns across everything registered in Lesson 8.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've labeled every piece of customer-sensitive data across the four systems we scanned, so access controls and compliance rules can now act on those labels automatically instead of relying on someone remembering which fields are sensitive. The audit confirms full coverage against what's actually in the catalog.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Every customer record across your core systems -- the SQL database, Salesforce, the warehouse -- now carries a clear, enforceable protection label wherever personal information actually exists, and we verified that coverage system by system. This is the control that makes PII protection something the system enforces automatically, not something that depends on someone remembering.

lessons.title: Capturing Lineage From Source to Executive Dashboard
lessons.summary: Tracing one real number on the executive dashboard backward, hop by hop, through the semantic model and the Fabric lakehouse to its original source -- using Purview's automated lineage.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: The final piece of this phase is lineage: using Purview's automated lineage, populated from Fabric and Power BI dataflow metadata, to trace one real number on the executive dashboard backward through the semantic model, the Fabric lakehouse, and back to its original source system. This lesson picks a specific number -- quarterly Active Customer revenue -- and proves, hop by hop, exactly where it comes from.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine looking at the final score on a scoreboard and being able to trace it backward: this point came from that shot, which came from that pass, which came from that player receiving the ball at that exact moment. Lineage does the same thing for a number on a dashboard -- it lets you click backward through every step that produced it, all the way back to the original system where the data first came from.
lessons.explainProfessional: This is automated data lineage in Microsoft Purview, built from scanning Fabric and Power BI dataflow and dataset metadata rather than hand-documented -- which matters because hand-documented lineage goes stale the first time a pipeline changes and nobody updates the diagram. The chain this lesson traces is the one this path's Fabric/Power BI coursework actually builds: source system, through an ETL/ELT process, into the Fabric lakehouse, up into a Power BI semantic model, and out to the executive dashboard's visual. Picking one real, specific number and walking it backward hop by hop is the test that proves the lineage graph is trustworthy, not just populated -- a lineage view nobody has ever verified against a real number is a diagram, not a control.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Pick one real, specific number to trace

The executive dashboard's "Q3 Active Customer Revenue" tile is the target: a single figure the VP of Finance will look at this quarter, built from the newly-approved Active Customer definition from Lesson 9.

## Step 2 — Open the lineage view from the dashboard end

In Purview's Data Catalog, open the asset for the Power BI executive dashboard report and select "View lineage." Purview's automated scan of the Power BI tenant surfaces the report's upstream dependency automatically -- no manual diagramming required.

## Step 3 — Walk the chain hop by hop

```
Executive Dashboard tile ("Q3 Active Customer Revenue")
  <- Power BI semantic model measure
  <- Fabric lakehouse table (customer + revenue, post-transform)
  <- Fabric dataflow / pipeline (ETL/ELT step, joining Oracle's
     Active Customer status to Snowflake's revenue fact)
  <- ORACLE_FIN.VW_CUSTOMER_SUMMARY (Active Customer status, the
     single-sourced Lesson 9 definition) + VERIDIAN_DW.FACT_SALES
     (net revenue)
```

Confirm each arrow in the Purview lineage graph actually appears -- no missing hop, no node that jumps straight from the dashboard to either source without the lakehouse and dataflow steps showing in between. A missing hop usually means a dataflow wasn't scanned, not that the dependency doesn't exist.

## Step 4 — Cross-check the number against the source, independently of the dashboard

```sql
SELECT SUM(revenue) AS q3_active_customer_revenue
FROM fabric_lakehouse.customer_revenue_curated
WHERE active_customer_status = 'Active'
  AND fiscal_quarter = '2026-Q3';
```

This curated Fabric table is where the dataflow already joined Oracle's `CUSTOMER_STATUS` to Snowflake's `net_revenue` -- `active_customer_status` here is populated from `ORACLE_FIN.VW_CUSTOMER_SUMMARY.CUSTOMER_STATUS`, not from the deprecated `VERIDIAN_DW.DIM_CUSTOMER.ACTIVE_FLAG`. Run this directly against the lakehouse and compare it to the dashboard tile's displayed value. A match confirms the lineage graph isn't just complete -- it's accurate: the number on the executive's screen really is produced by the chain Purview shows.

## Step 5 — Document the verified lineage as a governance artifact

Attach a short note to the dashboard asset in Purview: the number traced, the date verified, and the exact hop-by-hop chain confirmed. This turns a one-time spot check into a reusable reference the next audit or incident investigation can start from instead of re-deriving the chain from scratch.

## Step 6 — Flag any future change that should re-trigger this check

Note in the domain's governance log that any change to the Fabric dataflow feeding this lakehouse table, or any change to the semantic model's measure definition, should trigger a re-verification of this lineage trace -- lineage is a snapshot of the pipeline's current shape, not a permanent guarantee.

## Step 7 — Trace a second number to confirm the pattern, not just the one tile

Repeat the walk for a second dashboard tile -- "Q3 Units Shipped," sourced from the Product/Inventory domain rather than Customer -- to confirm the same five-hop pattern (source system, through an ETL/ELT step, into the lakehouse, up into the semantic model, out to the dashboard) holds across domains, not just for the one number this lesson started with. Finding the identical chain shape twice is what turns "this one number traces cleanly" into "this platform's lineage is reliable," which is the actual claim worth making to the Data Governance Council.

## Step 8 — Share the lineage view with the domain owners from Lesson 10

Send the VP of Finance's dashboard lineage trace to Priya Nair and David Chen, the Customer and Financial domain owners, so the people accountable for what these numbers mean have also seen exactly how they're produced. A business owner who has walked the lineage chain once is far better equipped to answer a board member's question about where a number comes from than one who has only ever seen the final tile.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Traced Q3 Active Customer Revenue on the executive dashboard backward through Purview's automated lineage: the Power BI measure, the Fabric lakehouse table, the dataflow, and back to its two real sources -- ORACLE_FIN for the Active Customer status and VERIDIAN_DW for the revenue amounts. Every hop showed up in the lineage graph with no gaps, and I independently reran the lakehouse-side aggregation to confirm it matches the dashboard's displayed number exactly.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We proved, end to end, that the number the VP of Finance is looking at on the executive dashboard is traceable all the way back to its original source system, with every step in between visible and verified. That's the kind of proof that holds up if anyone ever questions a number in an audit or a board meeting.
